lessons.title: Selecting an Apiary Site: Sun, Wind, Water
lessons.body: Choose a site that gets morning sun and afternoon shade. In hot African regions, hives facing east or northeast get early warmth to start foraging, but avoid full-day sun that melts comb. In cooler highlands, full sun is better to keep hives warm. Place hives where they are sheltered from strong winds. A windbreak of tall grass, shrubs, or a fence 2â3 meters away reduces wind stress and prevents hives from tipping. Avoid low-lying areas that flood; bees drown and hives rot. The site should be at least 100 meters from livestock pens and human footpaths to reduce disturbance. If you have a permanent water source like a stream or pond within 500 meters, that's ideal. Otherwise, provide a shallow water trough with stones for bees to land on. Never place hives under trees that drop sap or attract ants. Keep hives off the ground: use stands 40â50 cm high with legs, and grease the legs or use ash to deter ants. In areas with honey badgers, use strong metal stands or hang hives from trees. For easy access, leave 1â2 meters of clear space around each hive. If you keep multiple hives, arrange them in a row or circle with entrances facing different directions to reduce drifting. Start with 2â5 hives for a beginner. Record the site's sun direction, wind direction, and distance to water. A good site means healthier bees and more honey.

lessons.title: Leveling and Securing Hives
lessons.body: A hive must sit level side-to-side and slightly tilted forward (2â3 cm) so rain runs out and not into the entrance. Use a spirit level or a clear bottle half-filled with water to check. If the ground is uneven, dig a shallow trench or use flat stones under the hive stand. For a permanent apiary, pour concrete pads or use treated wooden posts set in the ground. Secure hives to stands with metal straps or strong rope to prevent theft and wind damage. In windy areas, drive a stake at each corner and tie the hive down. For top-bar hives, ensure the bars are level and tight; gaps invite pests. If using Kenyan top-bar hives, the legs should be at least 40 cm high and made of metal or treated wood. Grease the legs with used engine oil or place them in tins filled with ash to stop ants. Check that the hive entrance is clear and not blocked by grass. After securing, observe the hive for a day: bees should fly in and out freely. If they cluster outside, the hive may be too hot or too small. For Langstroth hives, use a hive strap around the whole box. In areas with elephants or monkeys, build a strong fence or hang hives from thick branches. Always secure the roof so it doesn't blow off. A well-leveled and secured hive reduces absconding and makes inspections easier.

lessons.title: Installing Packages and Nucs
lessons.body: Install packages and nucs in the late afternoon when bees are less active. For a package (a box of bees with a mated queen in a cage), first prepare the hive: remove 4â5 frames from the center, leaving a gap. Spray the package lightly with sugar syrup (1:1 water to sugar) to calm bees. Shake the bees into the gap, then gently place the queen cage between two frames, candy side up. Close the hive and leave them for 3â5 days. The bees will eat through the candy and release the queen. For a nuc (a small hive with 4â5 frames of brood, bees, and a queen), simply transfer the frames into your hive, keeping them in the same order. Add empty frames to fill the box. Do not smoke heavily; a little smoke is fine. Feed the new colony with sugar syrup (1:1) for 2â3 weeks to help them draw comb. Use a feeder inside the hive or a bucket feeder on top. In hot climates, provide shade and ensure ventilation. Check after 3 days: the queen should be laying. If not, look for the queen or eggs. In Africa, install during a nectar flow if possible, or when flowering plants are abundant. Avoid installing during dearth or heavy rains. If you buy a nuc, inspect it for pests like small hive beetles or varroa (if present in your area). Always wear protective gear. After installation, reduce the entrance to 2â3 cm to help the bees defend against robbers. Leave them undisturbed for a week, then inspect.

lessons.title: Routine Inspections and Record Keeping
lessons.body: Inspect your hives every 7â10 days during the active season, and every 2â3 weeks during dearth. Open the hive on a sunny, calm day between 10 am and 4 pm when foragers are out. Use a smoker with dry grass or cow dung to calm bees. Stand to the side of the entrance, not in front. Remove the roof and inner cover gently. Use a hive tool to pry frames apart. Check for: eggs and larvae (queen is laying), queen cells (swarming or supersedure), food stores (honey and pollen), pests (ants, wax moths, small hive beetles), and diseases (foulbrood, chalkbrood). Count frames of brood. A strong colony should have 5â8 frames of brood. Look for the queen; if you don't see her, look for eggs (tiny white specks). If no eggs, the colony may be queenless. Keep records: date, hive number, number of frames of brood, food status, queen seen (yes/no), pests, and actions taken. Use a notebook or a simple form. For example: '15/03/2025, Hive 2: 6 frames brood, 3 frames honey, queen seen, no pests, added super.' Records help you track colony health, predict swarming, and plan harvests. In Africa, where seasons vary, records show when dearth starts so you can feed early. Always clean your hive tool between hives with a flame or alcohol to prevent disease spread. After inspection, close the hive carefully and secure the roof. Limit inspection to 15â20 minutes to avoid chilling or overheating brood.

lessons.title: Repairing and Replacing Damaged Parts
lessons.body: Inspect hives monthly for damage. Common problems: broken frames, cracked boxes, holes in roofs, and rusted metal parts. Repair small cracks with wood filler or a mixture of sawdust and wood glue. For larger holes, cut a piece of wood to fit and nail it over the hole. Replace broken top bars or frames immediately; bees will build burr comb in the gap, making inspections difficult. Use a hive tool to scrape off propolis and wax before repairing. If a box is rotten, replace it with a new one. In Africa, termites are a major threat. Treat wooden stands and boxes with used engine oil or a borate solution (20% borax, 80% water) by painting or soaking. Check metal stands for rust; paint with anti-rust paint. Replace worn hive straps. If the roof is leaking, apply a new layer of tar felt or corrugated iron sheet. For Kenyan top-bar hives, ensure the bars are straight and not warped; replace warped bars. If a hive becomes infested with wax moths, remove affected frames and freeze them for 24 hours (if possible) or burn them. Clean the hive with a scraper and expose it to sunlight for a day. For small hive beetles, use traps or diatomaceous earth around the stand. Always keep spare parts: extra frames, boxes, roofs, and stands. A well-maintained hive lasts 10â15 years. In the rainy season, check for leaks weekly. After repairs, reassemble the hive and ensure it is level and secure. If a colony is too weak to defend a damaged hive, consider combining it with a stronger colony.

lessons.title: Winterizing and Spring Buildup
lessons.body: In Africa, 'winter' refers to the cool, dry season or the rainy season, depending on your region. In highlands, temperatures can drop below 10Â°C, and bees cluster. Prepare by reducing the entrance to 1â2 cm to keep out cold and robbers. Ensure the hive has 4â6 frames of honey; if not, feed thick sugar syrup (2:1) in a feeder. Wrap the hive with a black plastic sheet or sack to absorb heat, but leave ventilation holes. In hot, dry areas, 'winterizing' means providing shade and water. Use a white-painted roof to reflect heat. During the rainy season, tilt the hive forward more and ensure the roof is watertight. For spring buildup (or the start of the main nectar flow), stimulate the colony: feed 1:1 sugar syrup and provide pollen substitute (soy flour and brewer's yeast mixed with honey). Add a super or empty box when the colony has 7â8 frames of brood. Reverse boxes if the brood is in the lower box and honey above. Remove any queen cells if you don't want swarming, or make splits. Check for pests and diseases after the dearth. In Africa, buildup often coincides with flowering of key plants like acacia, citrus, or sunflower. Time your inspections to catch the flow. Provide clean water nearby. If you have multiple hives, equalize brood and food between strong and weak colonies. Record your actions. A strong spring buildup leads to a good harvest.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Hive Placement, Setup & Maintenance

This practical reference is written for the working African beekeeper â whether you manage five hives behind a homestead in Kakamega, fifty hives on a commercial acacia block in Tanzania, or a pollination service contracted to a mango estate in Ghana. Every recommendation below is framed around the business of bees: healthy colonies produce more honey, more splits, more pollination revenue, and more value-added products (beeswax, propolis, royal jelly). Placement and maintenance are not hobby details â they are the difference between a hive that pays for itself in one season and a hive that quietly dies and takes your capital with it.

Use this module alongside the six lessons in the course. The tables, diagram, and checklist are designed to be printed and carried to the apiary.

Site Selection: The Business Case for Getting It Right First Time

Moving hives after installation costs labour, stresses colonies, and loses foraging days. A site chosen on the criteria below will typically out-produce a poorly sited apiary by 30â60% in the first year, according to trials reported by the International Centre of Insect Physiology and Ecology (ICIPE) in Kenya. That is the difference between a marginal and a profitable enterprise.

Table 1. Apiary site scoring matrix (score each 1â5; aim for 30+ out of 40)
Criterion What good looks like (Africa context) Why it matters to the business
Sun East-facing entrance; 4â6 hours direct morning sun; afternoon shade in lowland tropics Early foraging = more nectar trips; reduces chalkbrood and small hive beetle pressure
Wind Natural or planted windbreak on the windward side; hives on stands 40â60 cm high Prevents comb collapse, reduces bee drift, protects brood in cold highland nights
Water Clean water within 300 m; a trough with floating sticks to prevent drowning Foragers spend less energy; colonies build up faster in dry season
Forage Continuous flowering within 1â2 km: acacia, citrus, sunflower, avocado, indigenous trees Determines honey yield and whether you can sell single-origin honey at a premium
Access & security Vehicle/motorbike reachable; away from footpaths; fenced or monitored Lowers harvest labour cost; theft is the single biggest loss in peri-urban apiaries
Drainage Gentle slope; never in a valley bottom or flood plain Waterlogged hives = mould, foulbrood, dead colonies after first heavy rain
Human & livestock buffer At least 50â100 m from homesteads, kraals, schools, and roads Reduces stinging incidents, legal risk, and pesticide drift from nearby farms
Pesticide risk Agreement with neighbouring farmers; avoid cotton, maize sprayed at flowering One spray event can wipe out a season's income

Sources: FAO Agricultural Services Bulletin 68/2, Beekeeping in Africa; ICIPE apiary management notes; Kenya National Beekeeping Institute extension materials.

Leveling, Securing and Installing Stock

Hives must sit perfectly level side-to-side and slightly tilted forward (2â3Â°) so that rainwater and condensation run out of the entrance rather than pooling on combs. In African conditions the three biggest setup failures are: hives placed directly on the ground (termites, ants, toads), hives unsecured against wind and livestock, and hives installed without a stand â which is the single cheapest upgrade with the highest return.

Install packages and nucleus colonies (nucs) in the late afternoon or early evening, when foragers are in and temperatures are falling. Feed 1:1 sugar syrup for the first 2â3 weeks if there is no strong nectar flow â this is not a cost, it is an investment that determines whether the colony draws comb before the dearth arrives. In East Africa, install during the long-rains build-up (MarchâApril) or short-rains build-up (OctoberâNovember) so colonies peak with the flowering season.

Routine Inspections and Record Keeping

An inspection is a business audit. Every visit should answer five questions: Is the queen present and laying? Is there brood in all stages? Is there enough stored food? Are there signs of disease or pests? Does the colony need space or a super? Record all five in a hive log â a paper notebook is fine, but a smartphone app such as BeeScanning or a simple spreadsheet will let you track yield per hive, per season, and calculate your true cost per kilogram of honey.

Table 2. Inspection frequency and seasonal maintenance calendar (tropical & subtropical Africa)
Season Inspection interval Key tasks Business action
Build-up (rains onset) Every 7â10 days Check queen, add supers, feed if needed, control ants Plan harvest labour; confirm market orders
Peak flow Every 10â14 days Add supers early, watch for swarming, keep water trough full Prepare extraction equipment; price honey
Harvest As supers cap Harvest only capped frames; leave 2â3 frames of stores per hive Weigh, label, batch; record yield per hive
Dearth / dry season Every 14â21 days Feed syrup or candy, reduce entrances, monitor absconding Value-add: candles, propolis, pollination contracts
Winter / cold highlands Every 21â30 days Insulate, close top vents, ensure stores, reduce entrance Repair hives, train staff, service equipment
Spring / pre-rains Every 7â10 days Reverse brood boxes, add space, split strong colonies Grow hive count; sell nucs as a second revenue stream

Sources: FAO, Beekeeping in Africa; Bees for Development, Beekeeping in the Tropics; Kenya National Beekeeping Institute seasonal advisory.

Repairing and Replacing Damaged Parts

Inspect stands, roofs, and boxes at every visit. Termite damage to stands is the most common structural failure in African apiaries â treat timber with used engine oil or plant stands on metal/stone footings. Replace warped or cracked boxes before the rains, not after. Keep at least one spare complete hive per ten hives in service so that a swarm or an emergency split can be housed immediately rather than lost.

Winterizing and Spring Buildup

In most of tropical Africa "winterizing" means preparing for the cool, dry or highland cold period and the dearth that accompanies it: reduce entrances, ensure 15â20 kg of stored honey or equivalent syrup, insulate the roof, and merge weak colonies. In Mediterranean-climate zones (Morocco, Tunisia, South Africa's Western Cape), true winter preparation applies: wrap or insulate, close ventilation, and check stores monthly. Spring buildup is the commercial growth phase â feed, expand, and split. A colony that goes into the flow with 8â10 frames of bees will out-yield one that goes in with four.

â  SAFETY WARNING â Africanized bees, agrochemicals, and fire
  • Africanized / aggressive colonies: Many African subspecies are highly defensive. Always work in pairs, wear a full suit and closed shoes, use smoke sparingly, and never open hives near homesteads, schools, or livestock. If a colony is persistently aggressive, requeen with a docile strain rather than tolerating it â the risk to workers and neighbours is a legal and reputational liability.
  • Agrochemicals: Never inspect immediately after a neighbour has sprayed. Confirm spray schedules before harvest and keep a written record â pesticide kills are the leading cause of sudden colony loss in commercial African apiaries, and documentation supports any compensation claim.
  • Fire: Smokers cause bush fires in dry savannah. Use a metal bucket for ash, never smoke in tall dry grass, and keep a fire extinguisher or water drum at the apiary.
  • Allergies: Keep an antihistamine and epinephrine auto-injector in the apiary first-aid kit; know each worker's allergy status before hiring.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Site scored 30+/40 using Table 1 before any hive is moved.
  2. Hives on stands 40â60 cm high, level side-to-side, tilted 2â3Â° forward.
  3. Windbreak established on the windward side; hives not in a wind tunnel.
  4. Water source within 300 m with floating landing sticks.
  5. Hives secured against wind, livestock, and theft (straps, fence, or lock).
  6. Inspection log updated every visit: queen, brood, food, pests, space.
  7. Spare hive ready per ten hives for swarms and emergency splits.
  8. Safety kit on site: suits, smoker, water/fire control, first-aid, antihistamine.

Further Reading (Free Official Resources)

  • FAO â Beekeeping in Africa (Agricultural Services Bulletin 68/2)
  • Bees for Development â free tropical beekeeping resources
  • ICIPE â Bee health and pollination research, Nairobi
  • Apimondia â international beekeeping congress papers and standards
  • USDA National Agricultural Library â Bees and Pollinators research portal

quiz.q: What is the ideal direction for a hive entrance in hot African regions?
quiz.explanation: Morning sun warms the hive early, encouraging foraging before the heat of the day.

quiz.q: How far should hives be placed from livestock pens?
quiz.explanation: 100 meters reduces disturbance from livestock and humans.

quiz.q: What is the recommended height for hive stands?
quiz.explanation: 40â50 cm keeps hives off the ground, deterring ants and moisture.

quiz.q: How can you deter ants from climbing hive stands?
options: A) Place water around the stand
B) Grease the legs or use ash
quiz.explanation: Grease or ash creates a barrier ants cannot cross.

quiz.q: What is the correct tilt for a hive?
quiz.explanation: A slight forward tilt lets rain run out and not into the entrance.

quiz.q: Why should hives be secured with straps?
options: B) To prevent theft and wind damage
C) To make them look neat
quiz.explanation: Straps prevent hives from tipping in wind or being stolen.

quiz.q: What tool can be used to check if a hive is level?
options: B) A spirit level or water bottle
quiz.explanation: A spirit level or a clear bottle half-filled with water shows level.

quiz.q: What should you do if bees cluster outside the hive after installation?
options: C) Check if the hive is too hot or too small
quiz.explanation: Clustering outside may indicate overheating or lack of space.

quiz.q: When is the best time to install a package of bees?
quiz.explanation: Late afternoon when bees are less active reduces stress and drifting.

quiz.q: How do you release the queen from a package cage?
options: B) Let the bees eat through the candy
quiz.explanation: The candy plug is eaten by bees over 3â5 days, releasing the queen safely.

quiz.q: What should you feed a new colony after installation?
quiz.explanation: 1:1 sugar syrup stimulates comb building and feeding.

quiz.q: How long should you leave a new colony undisturbed after installation?
quiz.explanation: A week allows the bees to settle and the queen to start laying.

quiz.q: What is a sign that a queen is laying?
options: B) Eggs and larvae in cells
quiz.explanation: Eggs and larvae indicate the queen is active and laying.

quiz.q: How often should you inspect hives during the active season?
quiz.explanation: 7â10 days allows you to catch problems like swarming or queenlessness early.

quiz.q: What is the best time of day to inspect a hive?
quiz.explanation: Midday when foragers are out and temperatures are warm.

quiz.q: Why should you keep records of hive inspections?
options: B) To track colony health and plan actions
quiz.explanation: Records help predict swarming, dearth, and harvest times.

quiz.q: What is a common pest of African hives?
quiz.explanation: All these pests can affect hives in Africa, though varroa is less common in some regions.

quiz.q: How should you clean your hive tool between hives?
quiz.explanation: Flame or alcohol kills pathogens and prevents disease spread.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a queenless colony?
quiz.explanation: Queenless colonies often have laying workers (many drones) and no brood.

quiz.q: How can you repair a small crack in a hive box?
options: B) Wood filler or sawdust and glue
quiz.explanation: Wood filler or a sawdust-glue mix seals cracks effectively.

quiz.q: What is a major threat to wooden hives in Africa?
quiz.explanation: Termites can destroy wooden stands and boxes if untreated.

quiz.q: How can you protect wooden hives from termites?
options: B) Treat with used engine oil or borate solution
quiz.explanation: Used engine oil or borate solution repels termites.

quiz.q: What should you do with frames infested by wax moths?
quiz.explanation: Freezing kills wax moth eggs and larvae; burning destroys severe infestations.

quiz.q: Why is it important to keep spare hive parts?
options: B) To quickly replace damaged parts
quiz.explanation: Spare parts allow immediate repairs, preventing colony stress.

quiz.q: In African highlands, what does 'winterizing' involve?
quiz.explanation: Reducing entrance and feeding helps bees survive cool, dry seasons.

quiz.q: What is a good sugar syrup ratio for winter feeding?
quiz.explanation: Thick syrup (2:1) provides more energy for clustering bees.

quiz.q: How can you provide water for bees in hot areas?
options: A) Leave a bucket of water
quiz.explanation: Stones allow bees to land and drink without drowning.

quiz.q: What is spring buildup?
options: A) Time of colony growth before nectar flow
quiz.explanation: Spring buildup is when the colony increases brood and population.

quiz.q: How can you stimulate spring buildup?
options: A) Feed 1:1 syrup and pollen substitute
quiz.explanation: Light syrup and pollen substitute mimic a nectar flow.

quiz.q: When should you add a super to a growing colony?
options: A) When 7â8 frames of brood are present
quiz.explanation: 7â8 frames of brood indicates the colony needs more space.
